Express consisted locomotive, baggage car, two coaches, sleeper; 61 passengers aboard per conductor's count at Cleveland. Damage to rolling stock assessed 14,200 dollars. Board recommended introduction block signal system over whole division and dismissal Caldwell; company carried out both within year.

The shipment was carried aboard the *Andromache*, a sailing barque of 598 tons register commanded by Captain Ruiz. The total weight of the ingots was 112 tons, with a total value of 8,400 pounds sterling.

Although the voyage was expected to take eleven days, the vessel was delayed for four days due to calms off Cape St. Vincent. The cargo was insured through Lloyd's at a premium of 1.75%.

The tea clipper Fiery Star cleared Foochow on 21 June 1866 carrying 1,207 chests of tea bound for London and drew 19 feet of water. Her owner, George Thompson of Aberdeen, had fitted her that season with Green's patent topsail yards, and she made 328 miles in her best day's run, a performance logged on 30 June in the China Sea. She anchored at Anjer on 8 July, took on 11 tons of coal and fresh provisions, and sailed again the same evening. The passage to the Lizard took 89 days, the ship arriving on 18 September, six days behind the Serica, which carried the season's first market. The Fiery Star's cargo sold at an average of two shillings and ninepence per pound. Her crew numbered 33 hands, of whom four were apprentices; one apprentice, David Bruce, kept a log of the voyage that was later deposited at the Aberdeen Maritime Museum.

The lighthouse at Cape Verde Point was commissioned on 3 March 1901 and was first lit by keeper Augusto Ferreira, who served there for eleven consecutive years. The tower is 34 metres high and is equipped with a second-order dioptric apparatus that shows two white flashes every fifteen seconds, visible at 18 nautical miles. The station burns kerosene at a rate of 460 litres per month, the fuel being drawn from a store built into the head keeper's cottage. A fog signal giving two blasts per minute was added in 1904 after the wreck of the barque Santa Ana, which struck the reef beneath the point on 9 July 1903 with the loss of seven hands. Log Diana of Hull kept by surgeon Dr. Charles Edward Smith dur Davis Strait fishery 1866, brig-rigged steam whaler 350 tons register, commanded by Captain John Gravill, left Hull 12 February crew 49 hands, 8 green hands shipped at two pounds ten per month, seasoned men drawing three pounds five. Crossed Arctic circle 3 March longitude 22 degrees west, made ice edge off Disko 19 March. First whale struck 2 April off Women's Islands yielded 12 tons oil and 9 hundredweight bone; second taken 17 April yielded 15 tons. End May catch four whales and 1,400 seals. 11 June nipped in ice Melville Bay lost rudder; temporary rudder fashioned from spare spars by carpenter within three days. Ship then beset drifted with pack 61 days, during which surgeon recorded first case scurvy 8 July and by middle of August 22 men on sick list. Lime juice run out, crew ate sorrel gathered Greenland coast when ship touched land 21 August. Three men died last week of August buried on shore. Diana worked free of ice 25 September reached Hull 11 October with 41 tons oil and 3 tons bone, paying voyage only by seal catch. The consulate report on the wool trade of the La Plata region was drawn up at Buenos Aires by Her Majesty's Consul, Mr. Edmund Monson, and was forwarded to the Foreign Office on 20 April 1875. It records that the clip of the season just closed was estimated at 68,000,000 pounds weight, against 61,000,000 pounds in the previous season, the increase being chiefly assigned to the extension of fencing on the estancias of the southern camps. Of this clip, some 26,000 bales were shipped to Havre, 19,000 bales to Antwerp, and 11,500 bales to Great Britain, the remainder being worked up in the local factories, of which fourteen were reported in operation against nine a year before.

The average price realized at the sales was elevenpence per pound greasy, a fall of twopence farthing on the year. The consul notes that the S.A. Bienvenida sheep, introduced by the Sociedad Rural in 1868, now numbered, by the best estimates, 3,000,000 head, and that their wool brought a premium of one penny per pound over the common criollo clip. Freight to London was taken at five eighths of a penny per pound, and to Havre at a halfpenny farthing; insurance on London account ran at thirty-five shillings percent. The report concludes with the observation that the drainage of the flooding lands near Dolores, begun in 1873 under the engineer Mr. James Baine, had reclaimed some 400 square miles of pasture, and that the railway from Tandil to the port, opened on 1 February of the present year, had already reduced cartage charges by two shillings per bale.

Commission appointed inquire into loss of Royal Charter steam clipper, sittings Liverpool begin 6 February 1860, before Mr. Tremenheere assisted by Captains Harris and Gray of the Board of Trade, Ship 2,719 tons register built on Clyde at Sandycroft in 1855, left Melbourne on 26 August 1859 with 388 passengers, crew 112, general cargo included 79,000 ounces of gold in 39 boxes consigned to London banks, Commanded by Captain John Taylor who had sailed with ship since first voyage, After passage of fifty-nine days against heavy westerly winds rounded Mull of Galloway morning 25 October took two pilots aboard at Point Lynas, That evening wind backed to the northeast increased to hurricane force by ten o'clock, Engines of 200 nominal horsepower worked to utmost but ship drifted stern-first toward coast of Anglesey, At half past one in morning of 26 October struck rocks half a mile east of Moelfre, First boat launched stove against ship's side, Raft constructed by carpenter Peter Gibson carried purser and twenty men to shore, Buoy line rigged by mate Joseph Rodgers saved further nineteen, In all 41 persons survived of 500 aboard, Gold with one exception went down with ship, Single box containing 1,640 ounces recovered from beach at Moelfre in November by local man Robert Williams, Commission found ship seaworthy and well found, Pilots had advised standing out to sea when wind shifted, Decision to anchor in Moelfre roads taken by Captain Taylor against that advice, Recommended establishment storm signal station at Point Lynas and lifeboat at Moelfre, Both provided within two years by Marine Board.

This is a log of the whaler Diana of Hull, kept by her surgeon, Dr. Charles Edward Smith, during the Davis Strait fishery of 1866. The Diana was a brig-rigged steam whaler of 350 tons register, commanded by Captain John Gravill. She left Hull on 12 February with a crew of 49 hands, of whom 8 were green hands shipped at two pounds ten per month, the seasoned men drawing three pounds five. She crossed the Arctic Circle on 3 March in longitude 22 degrees west and made the ice edge off Disko on 19 March. The first whale was struck on 2 April off the Women's Islands and yielded 12 tons of oil and 9 hundredweight of bone; a second, taken on 17 April, yielded 15 tons. By the end of May the catch stood at four whales and 1,400 seals. On 11 June the ship was nipped in the ice in Melville Bay and lost her rudder; a temporary one was fashioned from spare spars by the carpenter within three days. The ship was then beset and drifted with the pack for 61 days, during which the surgeon recorded the first case of scurvy on 8 July and, by the middle of August, 22 men were on the sick list. Lime juice having run out, the crew ate sorrel gathered on the Greenland coast when the ship touched land on 21 August. Three men died in the last week of August and were buried on shore. The Diana worked free of the ice on 25 September and reached Hull on 11 October with 41 tons of oil and 3 tons of bone, the voyage being a paying one only by the seal catch. The owners, Samuel and Charles Gourlay, declared the gross earnings at 3,860 pounds and paid each seasoned hand 19 pounds twelve shillings for the voyage.

This is a field dispatch from the survey of the Bengal Nagpur railway extension, written at Chanda on 29 November 1889 by the assistant engineer, Mr. Reginald Shaw, to the chief engineer at Calcutta. Shaw reports that his survey party, numbering 34 persons, including 12 chainmen and 6 sappers of the Madras Sappers, had completed the location survey of the 92-mile section from Nagbhid to Chanda on 22 November after fourteen weeks in the field. The line as located follows the Wyne Ganga valley for 41 miles, crosses that river by a bridge of seven spans of 150 feet at Karanja, and then takes the northern flank of the hills.

Shaw estimates earthwork for the whole section at 480,000 cubic yards, of which 62,000 cubic yards are rock excavation occurring in the eleven miles beyond Ballarshah. Three alignments were examined for the Karanja crossing; the adopted line is 1.7 miles longer than the southern route but avoids 90,000 cubic yards of rock and two well sinkings. He reports the country between Ballarshah and Chanda to be healthy except in the months of July and August, when fever this season carried off four chainmen. The party's expenses to date were 19,400 rupees against a sanctioned grant of 30,000 rupees. Shaw requests an additional 8,000 rupees for the next season, a theodolite to replace the one damaged at the Wyne Ganga crossing on 3 September, and the loan of a second survey elephant from the Chanda division because the party's own elephant had gone lame after the monsoon. He closes by noting that the levelling of the first 40 miles has been checked twice and agrees within 0.15 feet.

Three men died during the final week of August and were buried on shore.

The voyage yielded 3 tons of bone and 41 tons of oil; however, the voyage was only profitable due to the seal catch. Kipton Crossing railway accident evening 18 April 1891. Toledo express running twenty minutes late est. 45 mph struck stationary freight train shunted onto main line. Collision killed express engineer Michael O'Hara and fireman; injured nine passengers none fatally. Investigating board found station agent Oberlin James Caldwell failed to deliver order fixing meeting point Elyria. Express consisted locomotive, baggage car, two coaches, sleeper; 61 passengers aboard per conductor's count at Cleveland. Damage to rolling stock assessed 14,200 dollars. Board recommended introduction block signal system over whole division and dismissal Caldwell; company carried out both within year.

Company Silver Queen Proprietary empl 87 men underground, 44 on surface under mine mgr Daniel Callaghan, came from Kalgoorlie that April. Two winding engines 60 indicated horsepower each erected on surface; third on order from Mort's Foundry of Sydney cost 1,850 pounds. Disp further noted wages raised two shillings per shift following strike August; amalgam retorts yielded 3,100 ounces silver for the month.

Log Diana of Hull kept by surgeon Dr. Charles Edward Smith dur Davis Strait fishery 1866, brig-rigged steam whaler 350 tons register, commanded by Captain John Gravill, left Hull 12 February crew 49 hands, 8 green hands shipped at two pounds ten per month, seasoned men drawing three pounds five. Crossed Arctic circle 3 March longitude 22 degrees west, made ice edge off Disko 19 March. First whale struck 2 April off Women's Islands yielded 12 tons oil and 9 hundredweight bone; second taken 17 April yielded 15 tons. End May catch four whales and 1,400 seals. 11 June nipped in ice Melville Bay lost rudder; temporary rudder fashioned from spare spars by carpenter within three days. Ship then beset drifted with pack 61 days, during which surgeon recorded first case scurvy 8 July and by middle of August 22 men on sick list. Lime juice run out, crew ate sorrel gathered Greenland coast when ship touched land 21 August. Three men died last week of August buried on shore. Diana worked free of ice 25 September reached Hull 11 October with 41 tons oil and 3 tons bone, paying voyage only by seal catch. Commission appointed inquire into loss of Royal Charter steam clipper, sittings Liverpool begin 6 February 1860, before Mr. Tremenheere assisted by Captains Harris and Gray of the Board of Trade, Ship 2,719 tons register built on Clyde at Sandycroft in 1855, left Melbourne on 26 August 1859 with 388 passengers, crew 112, general cargo included 79,000 ounces of gold in 39 boxes consigned to London banks, Commanded by Captain John Taylor who had sailed with ship since first voyage, After passage of fifty-nine days against heavy westerly winds rounded Mull of Galloway morning 25 October took two pilots aboard at Point Lynas, That evening wind backed to the northeast increased to hurricane force by ten o'clock, Engines of 200 nominal horsepower worked to utmost but ship drifted stern-first toward coast of Anglesey, At half past one in morning of 26 October struck rocks half a mile east of Moelfre, First boat launched stove against ship's side, Raft constructed by carpenter Peter Gibson carried purser and twenty men to shore, Buoy line rigged by mate Joseph Rodgers saved further nineteen, In all 41 persons survived of 500 aboard, Gold with one exception went down with ship, Single box containing 1,640 ounces recovered from beach at Moelfre in November by local man Robert Williams, Commission found ship seaworthy and well found, Pilots had advised standing out to sea when wind shifted, Decision to anchor in Moelfre roads taken by Captain Taylor against that advice, Recommended establishment storm signal station at Point Lynas and lifeboat at Moelfre, Both provided within two years by Marine Board.

Lighthouse Cape Verde Point commissioned 3 March 1901, first lit by kp Augusto Ferreira served there eleven consecutive years. Tower stands 34 metres high; dioptric apparatus second order shows two white flashes every fifteen seconds visible at 18 nautical miles. Station burns kerosene at rate 460 litres per month, drawn from store built into head keeper's cottage. Fog signal two blasts per minute added in 1904 after wreck of barque Santa Ana struck reef beneath point 9 July 1903 with loss of seven hands. Point lies 6 kilometres north of fishing port Praia Seca. Telephone line to port completed in 1907. Ferreira succeeded in 1912 by asst. Joao Braz joined service 1898.

Annual rpt Submarine Telegraph Company year ending 31 December 1868 laid before shareholders general mtg offices Lothbury London 11 February 1869 chair taken by company's president Sir Charles Bright.

Rpt stated company now operated 1,940 nautical miles submarine cable of which 310 miles laid during year at cost 118,000 pounds comprising new Dover to Cape Grisnez circuit 26 miles and extension from Cromer to Hanstholm 284 miles.

Gross receipts for year 147,300 pounds increase 11,200 pounds over 1867 Continental messages contributed 96,400 pounds at an average of four shillings and twopence per message.

Total number of messages transmitted 412,000 daily average 1,127.

Working expenses stated 62,500 pounds leaving net profit 84,800 pounds directors recommended dividend seven percent absorbing 59,000 pounds and carrying 25,800 pounds to reserve fund which would then stand at 100,000 pounds.

Engineer to company Mr. Latimer Clark reported failures confined to two faults Dover cable — first 14 April caused by ship's anchor at Goodwins repaired in nineteen hours; second 3 August near French shore repaired in two days by company's steamer Investigator under Captain Wood.

Staff at date of rpt numbered 214 persons of whom 61 clerks employed at central station Lothbury working in three shifts of eight hours.

Mtg closed with vote of thanks to chairman carried unanimously.

The gross receipts for the year were 147,300 pounds, an increase of 11,200 pounds over 1867, of which the Continental messages contributed 96,400 pounds at an average of four shillings and twopence per message. The total number of messages transmitted was 412,000, being a daily average of 1,127. Working expenses were stated at 62,500 pounds, leaving a net profit of 84,800 pounds, from which the directors recommended a dividend of seven percent, absorbing 59,000 pounds, and the carrying of 25,800 pounds to the reserve fund, which would then stand at 100,000 pounds. The company’s engineer, Mr. Latimer Clark, reported that the failures of the year had been confined to two faults in the Dover cable: the first on 14 April, caused by a ship’s anchor at the Goodwins and repaired in nineteen hours; and the second on 3 August, near the French shore, repaired in two days by the company’s steamer Investigator under Captain Wood. The staff at the date of the report numbered 214 persons, of whom 61 were clerks employed at the central station in Lothbury, working in three shifts of eight hours. The meeting closed with a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was carried unanimously.

A commission appointed to inquire into the loss of the Royal Charter steam clipper held its sittings at Liverpool beginning on 6 February 1860, before Mr. Tremenheere, assisted by Captains Harris and Gray of the Board of Trade. The ship was the Royal Charter, a steam clipper of 2,719 tons register, built on the Clyde at Sandycroft in 1855. She had left Melbourne on 26 August 1859 with 388 passengers, a crew of 112, and a general cargo that included 79,000 ounces of gold packed in 39 boxes consigned to London banks. She was commanded by Captain John Taylor, who had sailed with the ship since her first voyage.

After a passage of fifty-nine days against heavy westerly winds, the Royal Charter rounded the Mull of Galloway on the morning of 25 October and took two pilots aboard at Point Lynas. That evening the wind backed to the northeast and increased to hurricane force by ten o’clock. The engines, of 200 nominal horsepower, were worked to their utmost, but the ship drifted stern-first toward the coast of Anglesey. At half past one in the morning of 26 October she struck the rocks half a mile east of Moelfre. The first boat launched was stove against the ship’s side; a raft constructed by the carpenter, Peter Gibson, carried the purser and twenty men to shore, and a buoy line rigged by the mate, Joseph Rodgers, saved a further nineteen. In all, 41 persons survived of the 500 aboard. The gold, with one exception, went down with the ship; a single box containing 1,640 ounces was recovered from the beach at Moelfre in November by a local man, Robert Williams.

The commission found that the ship had been seaworthy and well found, that the pilots had advised standing out to sea when the wind shifted, and that the decision to anchor in Moelfre roads had been taken by Captain Taylor against that advice. They recommended the establishment of a storm signal station at Point Lynas and a lifeboat at Moelfre, both of which were provided within two years by the Marine Board.

The librarian had received a parcel of books about natural history the previous day, which had been purchased at an auction for a small amount. She entered each volume into the catalogue, repaired a torn map using thin paper and paste, and placed the new arrivals on the shelf closest to the fire so that the members could find them.

The pilots kept watch from a wooden tower above the bar. Traffic at the mouth of the river was steady all week, and the log of boarding showed a greater number of vessels than in any month since the trade began. When fog came down, the station signaled with a horn and a bell, and while the weather remained foul no vessel grounded on the shifting sand.
